situation:
You are the membership analytics manager and the director of member experience at PULSEVOLT FITNESS CLUBS, a chain of forty fitness centers built over eighteen years. The founder and chief executive officer (judge) has asked you to weigh in before a decision that must be settled within the month. The founder is stepping away from daily operations and has signed a letter of intent to sell the company to a regional wellness investment group.

PULSEVOLT built part of its profitability on a data arrangement most members barely notice. Check-in records, class attendance, and workout metrics synced from members' wearables are aggregated and licensed to an outside wellness analytics partner, a practice disclosed in general terms within the membership agreement every member signs at enrollment. The revenue is modest against club dues but has grown steadily, and the buyer's due diligence team has flagged it as one of the assets it is valuing closely.

The current anonymization vendor strips names and account numbers for a low fee per record, and its contract renews automatically in two weeks unless PULSEVOLT cancels it first. A trade publication recently reported that a rival chain's data, scrubbed the same way, was partially re-identified by researchers who cross-referenced it against public fitness-app leaderboards. A newer vendor offers a stronger scrubbing method that would close that gap, but it charges nearly three times as much per record and needs six weeks to implement fully.

The founder (judge) wants a recommendation on which vendor PULSEVOLT should use going forward, and whether the current contract should be allowed to renew while the switch is arranged. Letting it renew keeps the licensing revenue intact for the closing valuation and avoids alarming the buyer with a sudden cost increase; canceling it before a replacement is ready would interrupt that income during exactly the weeks the sale is being finalized.

Neither option violates the membership agreement's disclosure language, and the sale itself has not yet been announced to staff or members. Even so, the founder does not want to hand a buyer a data practice that could become a headline six months after closing, and does not want to be remembered for scrapping a profitable, lawful arrangement over a risk that only a competitor has actually suffered. The recommendation has to hold up whichever way the timing falls.

The founder (judge) will greet you and your teammate at the start of the meeting and ask to hear your recommendation on how PULSEVOLT should handle the data vendor decision before the sale closes, along with the reasoning that supports it. After your presentation and any questions, the founder will thank you for your time and end the meeting.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the founder and chief executive officer of PULSEVOLT FITNESS CLUBS (judge). Business background is the same as the situation above. You have asked the participant team to recommend whether the club chain should let its current data-anonymization vendor's contract renew automatically or switch now to a costlier, more secure vendor before the pending sale of the company closes.

The judge will greet the participant team and ask to hear their ideas. After the presentation and the questions below, the judge will thank the participant team. The judge is not to make any comments after the event is over except to thank the participant team.
judgeQuestions: Why does the choice of vendor matter to the buyer completing due diligence on PULSEVOLT?
Why does the timing of the switch matter to the members whose data is involved?
Why would this decision matter to you personally as the founder, even after the sale closes?
